extracted.intended_audience: editors, writers, and copyeditors (users of the Chicago Manual of Style)
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed Chicago Manual of Style rules and explanatory guidance for punctuation (commas, semicolons, colons, question/exclamation marks, hyphens/en dashes/em dashes, parentheses) with examples and editorial notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with introductory quotation tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas are usually introduced when the quoted material is introduced by a phrase such as said, replied, or the like; commas are required regardless of the position of the explanatory text relative to the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: It was Thoreau who wrote, “One generation...”; She replied, “I hope you aren’t referring to us.” If the quotation is introduced by that, whether, if, or a similar conjunction, no comma is normally needed (Was it Stevenson who said that “the cruelest lies...”?). See related notes on location of comma relative to closing quotation marks and dialogue handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with quoted or italicized titles and expressions (appositive rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles or expressions set off with quotation marks or italics are usually treated like noun forms; commas are used or omitted as they would be with any other noun (i.e., use appositive/nonrestrictive rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set off the title with commas only if it is nonrestrictive and can be omitted without obscuring the identity of the noun (e.g., His favorite story in Joyce’s Dubliners is “Counterparts.” vs. Of her many favorites, “One Art” is the one she knows best.). Avoid the common mistake of always using a comma before a title following a noun; apply the appositive test (see 6.28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with direct questions embedded in a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct question included within a sentence but not enclosed in quotation marks is usually introduced by a comma and begins with a capital letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: She wondered, What am I doing? Legislators had to be asking themselves, Can the fund be used...?. If a question ends before the sentence does, no comma is required after the question mark (What am I doing? she wondered.). If awkward, rephrase as an indirect question (no question mark, no comma, no capitalization). See also guidance on capitalization and indirect questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with Jr., Sr., and generational suffixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas are not required with Jr. and Sr., and they are never used to set off II, III, and the like when used as part of a name; in an inverted name a comma is required before such an element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John Doe Sr. (no comma); Deer, Jason, III (inverted index entry requires comma). If a comma is used to set off Jr. or Sr., a second comma is normally required in the middle of a sentence (rephrase to avoid awkward possessives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with Inc., Ltd., and company abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas are not required with Inc., Ltd., and the like when part of a company’s name; articles and books should generally opt for consistent style rather than follow a company’s internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: QuartzMove Inc. was just one such company named in the suit. If a comma is used to set off the abbreviation, a second comma is normally required in the middle of a sentence (see 6.17); rephrase as needed to avoid awkward possessives. See also related cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with interjected 'not' phrases (antithetical elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phrase beginning with not is interjected to clarify a particular noun, commas should be used to set off the phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: We hoped the mayor herself, not her assistant, would attend the meeting. They want you, not him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with 'not... but' and similar constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: With interjected phrases of the type not... but or not only... but also, commas are usually unnecessary; commas (or a dash) may be used for emphasis or clarification at editorial judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples without commas: Works of art are created not by inspiration but by persistence. Being almost perfectly ambidextrous, she wore not one watch but two. If emphasis is required, an em dash or commas may be used (She was in the habit...—not only as a matter of personal pride but also...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with 'the more... the less' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is customarily used between clauses of the 'the more... the less' type; shorter phrases of that type rarely merit commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (comma): The more I discover..., the less I seem to care... Example (no comma for short phrase): The more the merrier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with parenthetical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If only a slight break is intended, commas may be used to set off a parenthetical element; if a stronger break is needed or if there are commas within the parenthetical, em dashes or parentheses should be used instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid awkward insertions (especially between an adjective and its noun); prefer rewording when necessary. Examples: All the test participants, in spite of our initial fears, recovered. The Hooligan Report was, to say the least, a bombshell. If stronger break needed, use em dashes or parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, indeed, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas—sometimes paired with semicolons—are traditionally used to set off conjunctive adverbs; when the adverb is essential to the meaning or emphasis, commas are usually unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A truly efficient gasoline-powered engine remains, however, a pipe dream. Indeed, not one test subject... But: If you cheat and are therefore disqualified, you may also risk losing your scholarship (no commas when adverb essential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with 'such as' and 'including' (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases introduced by such as or including follow restrictive/nonrestrictive principles: nonrestrictive examples are set off by commas; restrictive examples are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The entire band, including the matutinal lead singer, overslept (nonrestrictive). Words such as matutinal and onomatopoetic are best avoided (restrictive). Apply the same test as for appositives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with 'that is', 'namely', 'for example'
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of the type that is are traditionally followed by a comma; they may be better set off by an em dash or semicolon, or enclosed in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: There are simple alternatives—namely, reusable cloth bags. Keesler managed to change the subject; that is, he introduced a tangential issue. Note: i.e. and e.g. are preferred in parentheses or notes in formal writing and are followed by a comma there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with 'too' and 'either'
rubrics_metrics.description: The adverbs too and either used in the sense of 'also' generally need not be preceded by a comma; when 'too' appears in the middle of the sentence or clause, a comma can aid comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (no comma): I had my cake and ate it too. Anders likes Beethoven; his sister does too. Example (comma for clarity): She, too, decided against the early showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with direct address and greetings
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is used to set off names or words used in direct address; in correspondence, a comma typically follows the greeting (a colon may be used in formal correspondence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ms. Jones, please come in. Dear Lucien, ... At the beginning of a speech or formal communication a colon usually follows the identification of those addressed (Ladies and Gentlemen:). If the greeting itself is a direct address, two punctuation marks may be needed (the direct-address comma and the comma/colon after the greeting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas to indicate elision
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is often used to indicate the omission of a word or words readily understood from context; the comma may be omitted if the elliptical construction is clear without it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In Illinois there are seventeen such schools; in Ohio, twenty; in Indiana, thirteen. One student excels at composition, another at mathematics, and the third at sports (comma may be omitted if clear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas between homonyms for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: For ease of reading and editorial discretion, two words spelled alike but having different functions may be separated by a comma if such clarification seems desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Let us march in, in twos. Whatever is, is good. Use discretion; sometimes rewording is better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon to join independent clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: In regular prose, a semicolon is most commonly used between two independent clauses not joined by a conjunction to signal a closer connection than a period would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: She spent much of her free time immersed in the ocean; no mere water-resistant watch would do. Use semicolons sparingly and for a closer link than a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons with conjunctive adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain adverbs (however, thus, hence, indeed, accordingly, besides, therefore, etc.) used to join two independent clauses should be preceded by a semicolon rather than a comma; a comma usually follows the adverb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The accuracy of Jesse’s watch was never in question; besides, he was an expert... Kallista was determined...; accordingly, she made an appointment...

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon versus comma with 'then' between clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The adverb then is often seen between independent clauses as shorthand for 'and then' and is commonly preceded by a comma; using a semicolon is acceptable and sometimes preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Touch and hold the icon, then drag it to the trash. Or: Touch and hold the icon; then drag it to the trash. In imperatives a comma is more or less obligatory, though semicolon is strictly correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons before expressions like 'that is' and 'for example' when introducing an independent clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon may be used before phrases such as that is, for example, or namely when they introduce an independent clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples in the manual. Consider readability and alternative punctuation when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons before a conjunction in formal prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally an independent clause introduced by a coordinating conjunction is preceded by a comma; in formal prose, a semicolon may be used instead to effect a stronger separation or when the second clause has internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Frobisher had always assured his grandson that the house would be his; yet there was no provision for this bequest in his will. When in doubt, consider using a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons in complex series
rubrics_metrics.description: When items in a series themselves contain internal punctuation, separating the items with semicolons can aid clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The membership was as follows: France, 4; Germany, 5; Great Britain, 1; etc. If ambiguity seems unlikely, commas may be used instead. No additional semicolon is required if the sentence continues beyond the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the colon to introduce illustrative/amplifying elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon introduces an element or series illustrating or amplifying what has preceded it; between independent clauses it functions much like a semicolon but implies 'as follows'. Use a colon sparingly and only to emphasize that the second clause illustrates or amplifies the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The watch came with a choice of three bands: stainless steel, plastic, or leather. The colon may sometimes be used instead of a period to introduce a series of related sentences. Consider em dash as an alternative for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: In typeset matter, no more than one space should follow a colon; in some specific settings (source citations, biblical citations, ratios) no space should follow a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow context-specific conventions (see citation sections). See also general spacing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization after a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: When a colon is used within a sentence, the first word after it is lowercased unless it is a proper noun. When a colon introduces two or more sentences, or speech/quotation/question, the first word following it is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The steps are as follows: first, make grooves... (lowercase). Yolanda faced a conundrum: She could finish the soup... (capitalized because colon introduces sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colons after phrases like 'as follows' and similar introductory phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon is normally used after as follows, the following, and similar expressions when introducing lists or sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The steps are as follows: first... Kenzie’s results yield the following hypotheses: First, ... On the other hand, do not use a colon after namely or for example; use a comma instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colons to introduce quotations, dialogue, or direct unquoted questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon is often used to introduce speech in dialogue or to introduce a quotation or a direct but unquoted question when the introduction is a grammatically complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Michael: The incident has already been reported. The question occurred to her at once: What if I can’t do this? For quotations introduced with said/replied etc., commas are normal but a colon may be used for emphasis or to set up a block quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colons in formal communications/greetings
rubrics_metrics.description: At the beginning of a speech or a formal communication, a colon usually follows the identification of those addressed (e.g., Ladies and Gentlemen: Dear Credit and Collections Manager:).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For less formal correspondence, a comma may be used after the greeting (Dear Lucien, ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common misuses of colons (not always needed before lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon is not always required before a series or list; to merit a colon, the words that introduce a series must constitute a grammatically complete sentence. A colon should not be used where it intervenes in what would otherwise be a grammatical sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: The menagerie included: cats, pigeons... Correct: The menagerie included cats, pigeons... Exception: when the verb is elided or understood (Pros: accuracy and water resistance.). When in doubt, test whether the introductory words form a complete sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the question mark
rubrics_metrics.description: The question mark is used to indicate a direct question; it may also indicate editorial doubt or express surprise, disbelief, or uncertainty at the end of a declarative or imperative sentence in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Who will represent the poor? This is your reply? Use sparingly for nonstandard senses. See cross-references for rhetorical/question punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct versus indirect questions (question-mark usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A question mark is used to mark the end of a direct but unquoted question; an indirect question never takes a question mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Is it worth the risk? he wondered. (direct) He wondered whether it was worth the risk. (indirect). Single-word questions within a sentence (who, when, how) may omit the question mark and are sometimes italicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite requests disguised as questions (imperative style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A polite request phrased as a question does not always require a question mark; such formulations can usually be reduced to the imperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Will the audience please rise. Would you kindly respond by March 1. Alternatively: Please respond by March 1. But genuinely interrogative polite questions still take a question mark (Would you mind telling me your age?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of question marks and other terminal punctuation relative to quotes/parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: A question mark should be placed inside quotation marks, parentheses, or brackets only when it is part of the quoted or parenthetical matter it applies to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The ambassador asked, “Has the Marine Corps been alerted?” “Is it worth the risk?” he asked. See also rules on commas and quotation punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the exclamation point
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclamation point marks an outcry or an emphatic or ironic comment and should be used sparingly to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Heads up! We should all be so lucky! Use sparingly and consider tone; see related rules for rhetorical uses and punctuation pairing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical question as exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence in the form of a direct question may be marked as rhetorical by using an exclamation point in place of a question mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: How could you possibly believe that! When will I ever learn! Use this device to indicate strong rhetorical feeling rather than a neutral question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point in brackets as editorial protest or amusement (avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding an exclamation point in brackets to quoted matter to indicate editorial protest or amusement risks being interpreted as contemptuous or arrogant and should be avoided unless such sentiment is intended; it is not a substitute for sic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer other editorial notations; reserve sic for indicating an error in the source rather than using bracketed exclamation for attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of exclamation point relative to surrounding punctuation and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclamation point should be placed inside quotation marks, parentheses, or brackets only when it is part of the quoted or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The performer walked off the stage amid cries of “Brava!” She actually believes the seller’s claim that the MP3 sounds “as good as the uncompressed original”!

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hyphen, en dash, and em dash usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphen, en dash, and em dash each have specific appearances and uses; correct use of the different types is a sign of editorial precision and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to appearance and examples in the manual; see also chapter cross-references for hyphenation of compounds and word division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens in compound words and names and word division
rubrics_metrics.description: The hyphen is used in compound words and names and in word division according to specific rules (see chapter 7 sections on hyphenation and word division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult detailed hyphenation tables and rules (7.36-47, 7.81-89) and related sections for word-break conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens as separators (numbers, spelled-out letters, identifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to separate numbers that are not inclusive (telephone numbers, SSNs, ISBNs) and to separate letters when a word is spelled out letter by letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1-800-621-2376; 978-0-226-15906-5 (ISBN); “p-h-y-l-l-i-s.” For hyphens in URLs and email addresses, consult relevant sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash as 'to' for number ranges and continuing numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal use of the en dash is to connect numbers (dates, times, page numbers), signifying 'up to and including' (or through); for parallel construction, use 'to' or 'through' if 'from' precedes the first element, and use 'and' if 'between' precedes the first element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The years 1993–2000; In Genesis 6:13–21. Avoid using en dash where 'to' would be clearer in prose (She was in college from 2012 to 2016, not 2012–16). See cross-references for dates and number ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash for ongoing/unfinished number ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: An en dash may be used to indicate a number range that is ongoing (e.g., dates of serial publications or birth dates of living persons); no space intervenes between the en dash and any punctuation that follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The History of Cartography (1987–) ; Jack Stag (1950–). Use conventions consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash with compound adjectives (linking open or hyphenated elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: An en dash can be used in place of a hyphen in a compound adjective when one element is an open compound or when both elements are hyphenated compounds; this signals a link across more than two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly; often rewording is preferable. Examples: the post–World War II years; Chuck Berry–style lyrics. Prefer clarity for general readers; if awkward, reword to avoid en dash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single word or prefix joined to a hyphenated compound (use hyphen, not en dash)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single word or prefix should be joined to a hyphenated compound by another hyphen rather than an en dash; reword if awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: non-English-speaking peoples; a two-thirds-full cup (better: a cup that is two-thirds full).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviated compounds treated as single words (hyphen use)
rubrics_metrics.description: An abbreviated compound is treated as a single word, so a hyphen, not an en dash, is used (Chicago’s en dash sense does not extend to 'between').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: US-Canadian relations uses a hyphen (treated as single abbreviated compound).

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash linking campus locations (institutional preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some multi-campus universities use an en dash to link the campus location to the university name; usage varies widely and the institution’s stated preference should be followed when in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the University of Wisconsin–Madison; the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee. Others prefer commas or 'at' (the University of California, San Diego; the State University of New York at Buffalo).

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash line-break conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In printed publications, line breaks should generally be made after an en dash but not before (like hyphens); in reflowable electronic formats, let the software determine breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid carrying over a single character to the next line (e.g., an isolated number or dash). See cross-references for electronic formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash vs minus sign (use correct character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The en dash is sometimes used as a minus sign, but minus signs and en dashes are distinct Unicode characters and should not be substituted; using the correct character is especially important in mathematical copy and searchable electronic text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minus sign = U+2212; en dash = U+2013. Substituting characters may hinder searches and create typographic inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash uses as substitutes for commas, parentheses, or colons
rubrics_metrics.description: The em dash is versatile and used to set off an amplifying or explanatory element; it can function as an alternative to parentheses, commas, or a colon—especially when an abrupt break in thought is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: It was a revival of the most potent image in modern democracy—the revolutionary idea. Use em dash sparingly for emphasis; consider readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid nested em dashes (do not use em dash immediately within another em-dash set)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid confusion, the em dash should never be used within or immediately following another element already set off by em dashes; use parentheses or commas instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (avoid): The Whipplesworth conference—which had already been interrupted by three demonstrations (the last bordering on violence)—was adjourned promptly. If nested dashes would occur, restructure or use commas/parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash between noun(s) and pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash is occasionally used to set off an introductory noun or series of nouns from a pronoun that refers back to them and introduces the main clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Consensus—that was the will-o’-the-wisp he doggedly pursued. Broken promises, petty rivalries, and false rumors—such were the obstacles she encountered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes for sudden breaks or interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash or pair of em dashes may indicate a sudden break in thought or sentence structure or an interruption in dialogue; use ellipsis for faltering speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Will he—can he—obtain the necessary signatures?” “Well, I don’t know,” I began tentatively. “I thought I might—” “Might what?” she demanded. If the break belongs to surrounding sentence rather than quoted material, the em dashes must appear outside the quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes with expressions such as 'that is', 'namely', 'for example'
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash may be used before expressions such as that is or namely to set them off (parallel to commas or semicolons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cross-references provided in related comma/semicolon sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes and other punctuation (question/exclamation before dash allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A question mark or an exclamation point—but never a comma, colon, or semicolon—may precede an em dash. A period may precede an em dash if it is part of an abbreviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Without further warning—but what could we have done?—she left. Only if—heaven forbid!—you lose your passport should you call home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting comma when em dash used in place of comma
rubrics_metrics.description: If an em dash is used where a comma would ordinarily separate a dependent clause from an independent clause, the comma is omitted; likewise when an em dash indicates interruption at the end of quoted material, the comma before the speaker tag can be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Because the data had not been fully analyzed—let alone collated—the publication was delayed. “I assure you, we shall never—” Sylvia began, but Mark cut her short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes and line-break conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In printed publications, line breaks should generally be made after an em dash but not before; with a closing quotation mark immediately following the dash, do not break between the quotation mark and the dash. In reflowable electronic formats, let software determine breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also en dash and hyphen line-break guidance. Avoid orphaned single characters at line starts or ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes used in lieu of quotation marks for dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Em dashes are occasionally used instead of quotation marks to set off dialogue (as in some European languages); each speech starts a new paragraph and no space follows the dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format: —Will he obtain the necessary signatures? —Of course he will! Use this convention only where appropriate for the publication’s house style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes in lists, indexes, and tables (informal uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Em dashes are sometimes used informally as bullet-like markers in vertical lists or to organize subentries in an index or to indicate an empty cell in a table, but such usage is best avoided in formal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly; prefer formal list punctuation and table conventions for published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2-em dash usage for omissions or redactions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2-em dash represents a missing word or part of a word omitted to disguise a name or an illegible part of quoted material; spacing rules depend on whether a whole word or only part is missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “The region gives its — to the language spoken there.” (space on both sides for whole word missing) Admiral N— and Lady R— (no space when part of word missing). Do not confuse with blank lines intended for filling in (use underscore).

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-em dash usage in bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: In a bibliography, a 3-em dash followed by a period represents the same author(s) or editor(s) named in the preceding entry; use cautiously as it can obscure information and is best applied by publisher or manuscript editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chaudhuri, Amit. Odysseus Abroad. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 2015. ——. A Strange and Sublime Address. London: Minerva, 1992.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses—stronger than a comma and similar to the dash—are used to set off material from surrounding text and can enclose material that has no grammatical relationship to the rest of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: He suspected that the noble gases (helium, neon, etc.) could produce a similar effect. Use parentheses when the parenthetical material is tangential; consider dashes for emphasis and commas for slight breaks.
